title: Seven sons to the river
hook: seven sons are given to the river while a king keeps his vow of silence; at the eighth, he speaks
carry: moksha: release from the round of births
tomorrow: why did only one of the eight sons get to live?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pratipa, a father's warning, and Shantanu's word never to stop or question her. Keeping your word is dharma.

A son is born to the king and queen. And the queen carries the baby down to the river, and gives him to the Ganga's waters. As she does it, she says it's for his good. Shantanu watches from the bank, and says nothing. He remembers what he promised: never stop her, never speak harshly to her, or she leaves. Another son is born, and the same thing happens. And another. The text tells it plainly, without looking away.
screen: `A SON, GIVEN TO THE RIVER.` → `THE KING SAYS NOTHING.` → `ANOTHER SON. AND ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Seven sons, the text says, one after another, into the river. Every time, Shantanu stays silent, afraid that if he speaks, she'll leave him. Then the eighth son is born. As she carries this one toward the river, Shantanu can't hold it in. Don't kill him, he says. Who are you? Why do you kill your own sons? She stops. I won't kill this one, she says. But my time with you is over, as we agreed. And she tells him who she is: Ganga, the daughter of Jahnu, the text says. The sons were the Vasus, cursed to be born as men, and she has freed them as she promised. The scene can be seen more than one way. For Shantanu, these were his children, lost in front of him. For the Vasus, it was the release they begged for. The Mahabharata doesn't smooth this over; it lets the scene stay hard. But look at what the Vasus asked for: not more life on earth, but to be set free from a human birth, and Ganga's waters did it. Hindus hold on to that: her waters free and purify. The deepest freedom Hindus seek is moksha, release from the round of births itself, and for many, the Ganga is bound up with that hope. That's why families carry the ashes of their dead to her at Haridwar and Varanasi, and why a few drops of Ganga water may be placed on the lips of the dying. The son who lives carries the Vasus' power, and their word that he'll have no children. Ganga takes the child with her, and goes.
screen: `SEVEN SONS; AT THE EIGHTH, HE SPEAKS.` · `I AM GANGA. THEY WERE THE VASUS.` · `A SCENE THAT STAYS HARD.` · `THE VASUS WANTED RELEASE.` · then, large: `MOKSHA: RELEASE FROM THE ROUND OF BIRTHS.`

segments.voice: This is a hard story, so go gently. Pour a little water into a cup and hold it for a moment. Bring to mind someone or something you've lost; you don't have to find a hidden meaning in it, because some things stay hard. Then pour the water out slowly, the way families give ashes to the Ganga, and breathe beside whatever you feel.
Vasus. The gods cursed to be born as men, given to the river seven times, and spared the eighth when the king finally spoke.
Your line: moksha, release from the round of births. Tomorrow: why did only one of the eight sons get to live? See you tomorrow.

fork.reveal: the Vasus begged Ganga to free them from human birth, and her waters did. that's why many Hindu families entrust their dead to her, hoping for moksha, release from the round of births.

original.note: Sanskrit vasu: the Vasus are a group of gods; here, the sons Ganga freed in her waters.

chat.meaning: Ganga says the sons were the Vasus, freed from human birth as they asked. That's why Hindus trust her waters to free a soul, and hope for moksha, release from the round of births. For Shantanu they were his children lost; the story lets both stay true.

Ganga.meaning: the sacred river, and the goddess of the river

Jahnu.meaning: the one Ganga names as her father

Vasus.meaning: a group of gods, cursed to be born as men

moksha.meaning: release from the round of rebirth

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Ganga's sons given to the river; Shantanu speaks at the eighth; Ganga reveals herself)
